query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled, trace quantity of a microalloying element (for example, Nb) to the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of a cohesive, enriched intergranular phase along the lamellar colony boundaries. This modified interface is anticipated to reduce the propensity for microcrack nucleation and growth, thereby simultaneously enhancing room-temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the conventional processing baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies whose internal boundaries serve as sites for microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled microalloying addition (e.g., 1–2 wt% Nb) during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: The intervention is implemented under conventional processing conditions (similar cooling rates and heat-treatment timelines) ensuring that the addition remains at trace levels so as not to form excessive secondary phases while allowing preferential segregation to lamellar boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a nanometer-scale, Nb-enriched intergranular phase along lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition is expected to segregate to internal boundaries during solidification and subsequent thermal processing, thereby enhancing the cohesive strength of these interfaces. This reduces local stress concentrations and impedes microcrack initiation and propagation, leading to simultaneous increases in tensile strength (owing to more robust boundaries) and ductility (by curtailing catastrophic crack growth).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Nb-added alloy will exhibit significantly higher ultimate tensile strength and enhanced elongation at failure during room-temperature tensile tests, along with microstructural evidence of a modified intergranular phase at lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys processed conventionally, characterized by brittle behavior and limited tensile ductility due to weak lamellar colony boundaries prone to microcrack initiation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective when the microalloying concentration remains within an optimal range (around 1–2 wt%); concentrations outside this range may either not produce sufficient intergranular phase modification or could lead to detrimental formation of unwanted secondary phases. The effect is also contingent on processing parameters that favor Nb segregation rather than homogeneous distribution.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact optimal concentration of Nb and the detailed chemical composition and thickness of the enriched intergranular phase necessary to achieve the desired balance of strength and ductility. Additionally, interactions between Nb and the primary phases need to be carefully controlled to avoid adverse effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set with a 1–2 wt% Nb addition and one set using the standard composition (control). Process both sets under identical conventional conditions. Characterize the microstructure, particularly focusing on the lamellar boundaries, using electron microscopy and chemical mapping techniques. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to compare ultimate tensile strength and elongation to failure.
measurements: Electron microscopy (e.g., TEM/SEM) for intergranular phase identification
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for chemical mapping at lamellar boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if microstructural characterization fails to reveal a modified, Nb-enriched intergranular phase at the lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.
